claim: Rod photoreceptors of nocturnal mammals display a striking inversion of nuclear architecture.
source: Rod photoreceptors of nocturnal mammals display a striking inversion of nuclear architecture, which has been proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to dark environments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Falk et al., 2019; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009; Solovei et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: Nuclear inversion has been proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to dark environments.
source: Rod photoreceptors of nocturnal mammals display a striking inversion of nuclear architecture, which has been proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to dark environments.
evidence: This is a previously proposed hypothesis cited in the abstract and supported by references in the introduction (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).

claim: Retinal optical quality improves 2-fold during terminal development.
source: Here, we show that retinal optical quality improves 2-fold during terminal development, and that this enhancement is caused by nuclear inversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental MTF measurements and Strehl ratio calculations presented in Figure 3.

claim: The enhancement in retinal optical quality is caused by nuclear inversion.
source: Here, we show that retinal optical quality improves 2-fold during terminal development, and that this enhancement is caused by nuclear inversion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with TG-LBR mice where nuclear inversion is arrested, showing no optical quality improvement (Figure 3B).

claim: Improved retinal contrast transmission enhances scotopic contrast sensitivity by 18–27%.
source: We further demonstrate that improved retinal contrast transmission, rather than photon-budget or resolution, enhances scotopic contrast sensitivity by 18–27%, and improves motion detection capabilities up to 10-fold in dim environments.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral optomotor response experiments comparing WT and TG-LBR mice at scotopic light levels (Figure 4C).

claim: Improved retinal contrast transmission improves motion detection capabilities up to 10-fold in dim environments.
source: We further demonstrate that improved retinal contrast transmission, rather than photon-budget or resolution, enhances scotopic contrast sensitivity by 18–27%, and improves motion detection capabilities up to 10-fold in dim environments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments showing WT mice have up to 10 times greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts compared to TG-LBR mice (Figure 4E).

claim: The vertebrate retina requires light to pass through multiple cell layers prior to reaching the light-sensitive outer segments of the photoreceptors.
source: The structure of the vertebrate retina requires light to pass through multiple cell layers prior to reaching the light-sensitive outer segments of the photoreceptors (Dowling, 1987).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about retinal anatomy supported by a citation to Dowling, 1987.

claim: In nocturnal mammals, the increased density of rod photoreceptor cells demands a thicker rod nuclei-containing outer nuclear layer.
source: In nocturnal mammals, the increased density of rod photoreceptor cells demands a thicker (Němec et al., 2007; Peichl, 2005) rod nuclei-containing outer nuclear layer (ONL).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Němec et al., 2007 and Peichl, 2005.

claim: In mice, rods account for around 80% of all retinal cells.
source: For mice, where rods account for around 80% of all retinal cells (Hughes et al., 2017), this layer of photoreceptor nuclei is 55 ± 5 µm thick, thus creating an apparent paradox by acting as a more pronounced barrier for projected images prior to their detection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hughes et al., 2017.

claim: The layer of photoreceptor nuclei in mice is 55 ± 5 µm thick.
source: For mice, where rods account for around 80% of all retinal cells (Hughes et al., 2017), this layer of photoreceptor nuclei is 55 ± 5 µm thick, thus creating an apparent paradox by acting as a more pronounced barrier for projected images prior to their detection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a measured value reported in the manuscript.

claim: In inverted rod nuclei, heterochromatin is detached from the nuclear envelope and found in the nuclear center.
source: Interestingly, rod nuclei are inverted in nocturnal mammals (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Falk et al., 2019; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009; Solovei et al., 2013) such that heterochromatin is detached from the nuclear envelope and found in the nuclear center, whereas euchromatin that has lower mass density (Imai et al., 2017) is re-located to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B1.

claim: Euchromatin has lower mass density than heterochromatin.
source: Interestingly, rod nuclei are inverted in nocturnal mammals (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Falk et al., 2019; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009; Solovei et al., 2013) such that heterochromatin is detached from the nuclear envelope and found in the nuclear center, whereas euchromatin that has lower mass density (Imai et al., 2017) is re-located to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Imai et al., 2017.

claim: In inverted rod nuclei, euchromatin is re-located to the nuclear periphery.
source: Interestingly, rod nuclei are inverted in nocturnal mammals (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Falk et al., 2019; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009; Solovei et al., 2013) such that heterochromatin is detached from the nuclear envelope and found in the nuclear center, whereas euchromatin that has lower mass density (Imai et al., 2017) is re-located to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B1.

claim: Nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals.
source: Given that this nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals and correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei, it was proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to life under low-light conditions (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).

claim: Nuclear inversion correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei.
source: Given that this nuclear inversion is exclusive to nocturnal mammals and correlates with the light-focusing capabilities of isolated nuclei, it was proposed as an evolutionary adaptation to life under low-light conditions (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009).

claim: High-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture.
source: It is widely assumed that high-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture (Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004; Warrant and Locket, 2004) and often comes at the expense of image detail (Cronin et al., 2014; Warrant, 1999).
evidence: This is a widely held assumption in the field, supported by citations to Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004 and Warrant and Locket, 2004.

claim: High-sensitivity vision often comes at the expense of image detail.
source: It is widely assumed that high-sensitivity vision depends on optimized photon capture (Schmucker and Schaeffel, 2004; Warrant and Locket, 2004) and often comes at the expense of image detail (Cronin et al., 2014; Warrant, 1999).
evidence: This is a widely held assumption in the field, supported by citations to Cronin et al., 2014 and Warrant, 1999.

claim: Nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission rather than photon capture or resolution.
source: Here, we show that nuclear inversion affects a different metric of vision, namely contrast sensitivity under low-light conditions. In particular, we experimentally show that nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission, rather than photon capture or resolution.
evidence: This is demonstrated through MTF measurements (Figure 3), PSF measurements showing no resolution change (Figure 3E2), and diffuse transmission measurements showing no change in photon capture (Figure 3E3).

claim: Enhanced contrast transfer emerges from a developmental reduction of chromocenter number.
source: Advanced optical modelling and large-angle scattering measurements indicate that this enhanced contrast transfer emerges from previously coarse-grained (Błaszczak et al., 2014; Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009) changes in nuclear granularity, namely a developmental reduction of chromocenter number (Figure 1B1).
evidence: This is supported by FACS measurements showing reduced scattering with chromocenter fusion (Figure 1G, H), optical simulations (Figure 2D, E), and MTF measurements in TG-LBR mice with arrested chromocenter fusion (Figure 3B).

claim: In the absence of photoreceptors and their nuclei, 49% greater image detail is observed.
source: In the absence of photoreceptors and their nuclei, we observed 49% greater imaged detail (cut-off chosen at 50% residual contrast, Figure 1B3).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements comparing WT and Rd1/Cpfl1-KO mice retinae, shown in Figure 1B3.

claim: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential.
source: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential (Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000), while photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides (Enoch, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000.

claim: Photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides.
source: Photoreceptor nuclei contain highly compacted and molecularly dense DNA with significant light-scattering potential (Drezek et al., 2003; Marina et al., 2012; Mourant et al., 2000), while photoreceptor segments have been described as image-preserving waveguides (Enoch, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Enoch, 1961.

claim: Light propagation in the mouse retina is significantly impacted by the highly abundant rod nuclei of the ONL.
source: These findings suggest that light propagation in the mouse retina is significantly impacted, if not dominated, by the highly abundant rod nuclei of the ONL.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental finding that removing the ONL increases image detail by 49% (Figure 1B3).

claim: Cells isolated from the mouse retina scatter substantially less light than neurons of the brain and cultured neuroblastoma cells.
source: These measurements revealed that cells isolated from the mouse retina known to typically consist of ~80% rod photoreceptor cells (Hughes et al., 2017), scatter substantially less light than neurons of the brain and cultured neuroblastoma cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements comparing different cell types, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Volume-specific light scattering is noticeably lower in retinal cells.
source: Using forward scattering as a measure of cell size indicates that side scattering normalized by volume (volume-specific light scattering) is also noticeably lower in retinal cells (Figure 1C, inset).
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Retinal cells are optically specialized, as they scatter less light for a given size.
source: This suggests that retinal cells are indeed optically specialized, as they scatter less light for a given size.
evidence: This is inferred from the FACS measurements showing lower volume-specific scattering in retinal cells (Figure 1C).

claim: The unique optical property of rod cells could stem from the unusually dense packing of the heterochromatin in the centre of their nuclei.
source: This unique property for the rod cells could stem from the unusually dense packing of the heterochromatin in the centre of their nuclei, which notably even excludes free GFP molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by microscopy data showing GFP exclusion from dense chromatin regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Sideward scattering was significantly reduced in adult retinal nuclei compared to the intermediate developmental stage.
source: In stark contrast however, sideward scattering, with a strong potential to diminish image contrast, was significantly reduced in adult retinal nuclei compared to the intermediate developmental stage (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements comparing P25 and adult retinal nuclei, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Nuclei with the lowest number of chromocenters scatter the least amount of light.
source: In particular, those nuclei with the lowest number of chromocenters were found to scatter the least amount of light.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of sorted nuclei from P25 retinae shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A wave-optical Mie model of light-scattering by refractive chromocenters closely reproduced the trend of light scattering reduction with chromocenter fusion.
source: In support of this experimental quantification, a wave-optical Mie model of light-scattering by refractive chromocenters closely reproduced the trend of light scattering reduction with chromocenter fusion (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on theoretical Mie scattering calculations shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In TG-LBR mice, heterochromatin remains anchored at the lamina which prevents the complete fusion of chromocenters.
source: To establish whether rod nuclear inversion is required to cause the developmental reduction in light scattering, we used a transgenic mouse model (TG-LBR) in which heterochromatin remains anchored at the lamina which in turn prevents the complete fusion of chromocenters (Figure 2A1, A2 and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Solovei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the TG-LBR mouse model described in Solovei et al., 2013 and illustrated in Figures 2A1, A2, B.

claim: In TG-LBR retinae, more than 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested.
source: FACS experiments of nuclei from TG-LBR retinae, in which > 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), revealed significantly increased light scattering (Figure 2C, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on quantification of LBR-positive nuclei shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TG-LBR retinae revealed significantly increased light scattering.
source: FACS experiments of nuclei from TG-LBR retinae, in which > 70% of the nuclei are successfully arrested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), revealed significantly increased light scattering (Figure 2C, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The global maximum of the side-scattering in TG-LBR nuclei was re-located precisely to the position characteristic of nuclei isolated from WT pups at P14.
source: Specifically, the global maximum of the side-scattering was re-located precisely to the position that is characteristic of nuclei isolated from WT pups at P14, which possess a similar number of chromocenters as inversion arrested nuclei (compare Figure 2B,C, Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is based on comparison of FACS data shown in Figures 2B, C, 1F, and G.

claim: The reduction of light scattering with chromocenter number is causal.
source: Because inhibition of chromocenter fusion leads to specific increase in scattering, we conclude that the reduction of light scattering with chromocenter number is causal.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental finding that preventing chromocenter fusion in TG-LBR mice increases light scattering (Figure 2C).

claim: Large-angle scattering monotonically decreases when 10 chromocenters successfully fuse into one.
source: These simulations suggest that especially the large-angle scattering (cumulative scattering signal at angles > 30 deg) monotonically decreases when 10 chromocenters successfully fuse into one (Figure 2D2 and E).
evidence: This is based on computational simulations of light propagation through the ONL shown in Figure 2D2 and E.

claim: The effect of reduced scattering can be explained by a reduction of volume-specific scattering for weak scatterers in the size regime slightly above one wavelength of light.
source: Physically, this effect of reduced scattering can be explained by a reduction of volume-specific scattering for weak scatterers in the size regime slightly above one wavelength of light, similar to scattering reduction techniques proposed for transparent sea animals (Johnsen, 2012) (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations shown in Figure 2F, G and supported by a citation to Johnsen, 2012.

claim: A decreased geometric scattering cross section after fusion leads to reduced scattering-induced veil that helps to prevent contrast losses.
source: Furthermore, a minimal optical ONL model reconstituted from suspended beads of different size but same volume fraction (Supplementary Methods) illustrates how a decreased geometric scattering cross section after fusion leads to reduced scattering-induced veil that helps to prevent contrast losses (Figure 2H and inset).
evidence: This is based on an optical reconstitution experiment using silica beads shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development.
source: Strikingly, we found that wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development, with adult retinae showing consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14) in which rod nuclei still possess around five chromocenters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements comparing adult and P14 WT retinae shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Adult retinae show consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14).
source: Strikingly, we found that wildtype retinae improve contrast transmission throughout terminal development, with adult retinae showing consistently elevated MTFs compared to intermediate developmental stages (P14) in which rod nuclei still possess around five chromocenters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The monotonic decay of retina-transmitted contrast indicates scattering-induced veil, rather than a frequency cut-off, to be the cause of contrast loss.
source: The monotonic decay of retina-transmitted contrast indicates scattering-induced veil, rather than a frequency cut-off to be the cause of contrast loss (Figure 3A,B Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the shape of the MTF curves shown in Figures 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: The retina matures towards increasing optical quality during latest developmental stages, with chromocenter fusion as a putative mechanism of veil reduction.
source: Collected from >1300 high resolution images, this data reveals that, similar to the lens (Tkatchenko et al., 2010), the retina matures towards increasing optical quality during latest developmental stages, with chromocenter fusion as a putative mechanism of veil reduction.
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements across development and comparison with TG-LBR mice, supported by a citation to Tkatchenko et al., 2010.

claim: Developmental improvements in optical quality do not occur in retinae in which rod nuclei are transgenically arrested in development and maintain 4–5 chromocenters.
source: These improvements in optical quality do not occur in retinae in which rod nuclei are transgenitically arrested in development and maintain 4–5 chromocenters. TG-LBR mouse (N = 18 animals) compared to WT reference (N = 19 animals), N = 1950 images in total.
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements in TG-LBR mice shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Strehl ratio of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14).
source: With regards to our MTF measurements, we that find the Strehl ratio (computed using the measurements in the spatial frequency range of 0–2 cycles/deg) of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14) in which chromocenters fusion was not completed, and similarly 1.91 ± 0.14 fold (ratio of means ± SEM) improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae (p=3.4055e-08) in which chromocenter fusion was deliberately arrested (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on Strehl ratio calculations from MTF data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Strehl ratio of a fully developed retina is 1.91 ± 0.14 fold improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae.
source: With regards to our MTF measurements, we that find the Strehl ratio (computed using the measurements in the spatial frequency range of 0–2 cycles/deg) of a fully developed retina is increased 2.00 ± 0.15 fold compared to that of pups (P14) in which chromocenters fusion was not completed, and similarly 1.91 ± 0.14 fold (ratio of means ± SEM) improved compared to TG-LBR adult retinae (p=3.4055e-08) in which chromocenter fusion was deliberately arrested (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on Strehl ratio calculations from MTF data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The resulting image at the back of the WT retina had a near two-fold (1.79 ± 0.38) higher peak intensity compared to the TG-LBR retina.
source: We found that the resulting image at the back of the WT retina had a near two-fold (1.79 ± 0.38, mean ± SD) higher peak intensity compared to the TG-LBR retina (Figure 3 E1 & E2, N = 119, N = 121, measured in at a total of 6 animals).
evidence: This is based on PSF measurements shown in Figure 3E1 and E2.

claim: The measured resolution based on full-width half maximum (FWHM) of the PSF did not show any differences between WT and TG-LBR retinae.
source: The measured resolution based on full-width half maximum (FWHM) of the PSF, however, did not show any differences (4.32 ± 2.38 μm, 3.75 ± 2.01 μm, mean ± SD for WT and TG-LBR retinae respectively, Figure 3 E2), especially no changes that could physiologically impact acuity, which is known to be significantly lower in mouse.
evidence: This is based on PSF measurements shown in Figure 3E2.

claim: Nuclear inversion enhances contrast transmission through the retina but is unlikely to benefit acuity.
source: In addition to independently corroborating our MTF measurements, these results emphasize that nuclear inversion enhances contrast transmission through the retina but is unlikely to benefit acuity.
evidence: This is inferred from the PSF measurements showing no change in resolution (Figure 3E2) despite improved peak intensity.

claim: Contrast is lost due to the generation of image veil from side scattering.
source: From a mechanistic point of view, these measurements indicate that contrast is lost due to the generation of image veil from side scattering, which overcasts attenuated, but otherwise unchanged signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of MTF measurements, PSF measurements, and scattering data.

claim: Despite differential image signal, the overall photon arrival at the photoreceptor outer segments remains unchanged between WT and TG-LBR retinae.
source: Accordingly, when comparing the integrated absolute transmission through rhodopsin-bleached retinae in dedicated experiments (Supplementary methods), we found near identical transmission values for WT and inversion arrested retinae (Figure 3 E3, TWT74 ± 8%, TLBR = 72 ± 5%, mean ± SD), which emphasizes that despite differential image signal, the overall photon arrival at the photoreceptor outer segments, remains unchanged.
evidence: This is based on diffuse transmission measurements shown in Figure 3E3.

claim: Nuclear inversion results in cat images becoming visible considerably earlier compared to mice that lack nuclear inversion (0.70 vs 0.45 meters).
source: Nuclear inversion results in cat images becoming visible considerably earlier compared to mice that lack nuclear inversion (0.70 vs 0.45 meters, at a given arbitrary noise threshold).
evidence: This is based on micro-projection experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Contrast sensitivity did not differ significantly between WT and TG-LBR mice at photopic light condition (70 Lux).
source: Firstly, contrast sensitivity assessed by the animal's ability to detect moving stripes, did not differ significantly (p=0.5307, two sample t test) between the two genotypes at photopic light condition (70 Lux – the typical brightness of monitor).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4B (left).

claim: At 20 mLux, WT and TG-LBR mice showed comparable responses for coarse stimuli.
source: At 20 mLux, which is the range of brightness in moonlight (Kyba et al., 2017), we again found comparable responses for coarse stimuli (wide large contrast stripes) suggesting equally functional rod-based vision in TG-LBR and WT mice (Figure 4B, right) without noticeable differences in absolute sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4B (right).

claim: Visual behavior under the displayed scotopic conditions fully relies on the functionality of the rod pathway.
source: Furthermore, mice deficient of rhodopsin (Rho-/-) (Humphries et al., 1997; Jaissle et al., 2001) confirmed that visual behavior under the displayed scotopic conditions fully relies on the functionality of the rod pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on control experiments with Rho-/- mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At 20 mLux, the overall sensitivity of WT mice is 22% higher than TG-LBR mice.
source: At 20mLux we observed an 18% greater AULC for WT mice compared with TG-LBR mice (p=0.00081).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4C. Note: The abstract states 18-27%, and the text mentions 18% at 20mLux.

claim: At 2 mLux, the difference in AULC values between WT and TG-LBR mice was 27%.
source: At even lower light intensities (2mLux, comparable to a starry night), the difference in AULC values was even greater (ratio 27%, p=0.0047) albeit at lower absolute sensitivities, which agrees with reported values for WT mice (Alam et al., 2015; Prusky et al., 2000; Prusky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The most significant differences in contrast sensitivity occur above 0.15 cycles/degree.
source: The most significant differences in the contrast sensitivity occur above 0.15 cycles/degree (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the regime close to the visual acuity (0.26–0.30 cycles/degree), WT mice show up to 10 times greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts compared to mice with inversion arrested rod nuclei.
source: Especially, in the regime close to the visual acuity (0.26–0.30 cycles/degree), WT mice show up to 10 times (p<0.0001) greater positive response rates at intermediate contrasts (Figure 4E) compared to mice with inversion arrested rod nuclei.
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At 90–100% contrasts, WT mice have a near 6-fold reduced risk to miss a stimulus compared to TG-LBR mice.
source: Moreover, at 90–100% contrasts, where WT mice approach a maximum responsiveness, we observed a near 6-fold reduced risk to miss a stimulus for WT compared to TG-LBR mice (false negative rates 11% WT, 59% TG-LBR).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The 18–27% difference in contrast sensitivity goes together with a 26% higher Strehl ratio in WT retinae when evaluated in the relevant frequency regime (0–0.36 cycles/degree).
source: Specifically, the 18–27% difference in contrast sensitivity goes together with a 26% higher Strehl ratio in WT retinae when evaluated in the relevant frequency regime (0–0.36 cycles/degree).
evidence: This is based on comparison of behavioral data (Figure 4C) with MTF-derived Strehl ratios.

claim: At low light levels, contrast sensitivity may be directly limited by contrast transmission through the retina.
source: This suggests that at low light levels, contrast sensitivity may be directly limited by contrast transmission through the retina, and that a reduction of contrast sensitivity in mice with non-inverted rod nuclei may be explained by increased contrast losses in the retina.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MTF measurements and behavioral sensitivity.

claim: With equal image contrast at the level of the photoreceptor segments, visual competence of LBR mice was rescued and becomes near identical to that of WT mice.
source: Strikingly, we found that with equal image contrast at the level of the photoreceptor segments, visual competence of LBR mice was rescued and becomes near identical to that of WT mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments where displayed contrasts were adjusted to pre-compensate for differential retinal contrast loss, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Improved retinal contrast transmission is sufficient to explain increased contrast sensitivity in mice.
source: Thus, improved retinal contrast transmission is indeed sufficient to explain increased contrast sensitivity in mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments.
source: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments, and often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout (Warrant, 1999; Warrant, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Warrant, 1999 and Warrant, 2017.

claim: Nocturnal vision often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout.
source: Nocturnal vision is known to rely on highly efficient light capture, both at the level of the lens and photoreceptor outer segments, and often compromises spatio-temporal resolution by summation strategies of neuronal readout (Warrant, 1999; Warrant, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Warrant, 1999 and Warrant, 2017.

claim: It is the direction into which light is scattered inside retinal tissue that translates into differential contrast sensitivity.
source: Centrally, we show that it is the direction into which light is scattered inside retinal tissue that translates into differential contrast sensitivity.
evidence: This is a central conclusion based on the combination of scattering measurements, simulations, and behavioral data.

claim: The forward scattering characteristic of inverted nuclei mainly suppresses light scattering by nuclear substructure towards large angles, thus preventing image veil and contrast reduction.
source: Specifically, we find that the forward scattering characteristic of inverted nuclei (Kreysing et al., 2010; Solovei et al., 2009) mainly suppresses light scattering by nuclear substructure towards large angles, thus preventing image veil and contrast reduction resulting from it.
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements (Figure 1F, G), simulations (Figure 2D2, E), and MTF measurements (Figure 3).

claim: Chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus.
source: As an example, chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus (Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017) and LBR downregulation might even be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei (Stephens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2019.

claim: LBR downregulation might be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei.
source: As an example, chromatin distribution is known to have the potential to modulate the mechanical properties of the nucleus (Kirby and Lammerding, 2018; Miroshnikova et al., 2017; Stephens et al., 2017) and LBR downregulation might even be required for shape changes enabling efficient packing of nuclei (Stephens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 2019.

claim: The increase in intensity of a point stimulus at the photoreceptor level could aid a thresholded or otherwise non-linear readout of rod cells.
source: Lastly, although the size of the PSF is beyond the acuity limit of nocturnal vision, the increase in intensity of a point stimulus at the photoreceptor level could aid a thresholded or otherwise non-linear readout of rod cells, a long-standing hypothesis in the field of visual neuroscience (Barlow, 1956; Field and Rieke, 2002; Nelson, 2017) which was substantiated by the use of quantum-based single-photon sources (Tinsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Barlow, 1956; Field and Rieke, 2002; Nelson, 2017; Tinsley et al., 2016.

claim: The larger spacing of photoreceptor segments in the diurnal retina significantly reduces ONL thickness.
source: Firstly, the larger spacing of photoreceptor segments in the diurnal retina significantly reduces ONL thickness (Solovei et al., 2009; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015; Werner and Chalupa, 2004; Williams and Moody, 2004) and thereby the risk of scattering induced veil and loss of image contrast.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Solovei et al., 2009; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015; Werner and Chalupa, 2004; Williams and Moody, 2004.

claim: Shot-noise that accounts for image granularity becomes less of a problem with increasing light levels.
source: Furthermore, as is well known from photography, shot-noise that accounts for image granularity (Barlow, 1956; de Vries, 1943; Rose, 1948) becomes less of a problem with increasing light levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Barlow, 1956; de Vries, 1943; Rose, 1948.

claim: Million-fold higher light intensities during the day imply a higher safety margin from the noise floor.
source: Million-fold higher light intensities during the day imply a higher safety margin from this noise floor (Warrant, 1999), (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G), as required for neural mechanisms of contrast enhancement to function (Artal et al., 2004; Flevaris and Murray, 2015; Hess et al., 1998; Shevell et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Warrant, 1999; Artal et al., 2004; Flevaris and Murray, 2015; Hess et al., 1998; Shevell et al., 1992.

claim: Although nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission via reduced image veil, resolution remains largely unaffected.
source: Last, but not least, our measurements show that, although nuclear inversion improves retinal contrast transmission via reduced image veil, resolution, the limiting factor for high acuity diurnal vision, remains largely unaffected.
evidence: This is based on PSF measurements showing no change in resolution (Figure 3E2).

claim: Reduced efficiency of canonical DNA repair mechanisms in highly condensed chromocenters could mean a significant disadvantage in the diurnal retina.
source: Besides a reduced need for inverted photoceptor nuclei in diurnal mammals, reduced efficiency of canonical DNA repair mechanisms (Frohns et al., 2014) in highly condensed chromocenters, could mean a significant disadvantage in the diurnal retina and susceptibility to stress and degeneration (Boudard et al., 2011; Dyer, 2016), could also mean a significantly higher cost for inverted nuclei in diurnal species, as their retinae are intrinsically strongly exposed to high-energy, ultra-violet photons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Frohns et al., 2014; Boudard et al., 2011; Dyer, 2016.

claim: Rod nuclear inversion is necessary and sufficient to explain optically enhanced contrast sensitivity in mice.
source: In conclusion, we showed that rod nuclear inversion is necessary and sufficient to explain optically enhanced contrast sensitivity in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combination of all experimental results including MTF measurements, behavioral tests, and rescue experiments.

claim: Downregulation of the lamina tether LBR enables fusion of mobilized chromocenters and thereby an architectural inversion of mouse rod nuclei.
source: Downregulation of the lamina tether LBR (yellow) enables fusion of mobilized chromocenters and thereby an architectural inversion of mouse rod nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B1 and supported by the TG-LBR experiments.

claim: The inner retina alone transmits approximately 50% more image detail than the full retina.
source: Quantification of image transmission shows that the inner retina alone (Rd1/Cpfl1-KO, N = 5) transmits approximately 50% more image detail than the full retina (N = 11), suggesting significant image degradation in the thick outer nuclear layer.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B3.

claim: Volume-specific light scattering is significantly reduced in the retinal cell nuclei.
source: Volume-specific light scattering is significantly reduced in the retinal cell nuclei.
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Quantification of reduced scattering with chromocenter number is sufficiently explained by a wave optical model of light scattering.
source: Quantification of reduced scattering with chromocenter number is sufficiently explained by a wave optical model of light scattering n = 38 nuclei.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with Mie scattering calculations shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In inverted rod nuclei, the chromatin of the central chromocenter and the surrounding shell of LINE-rich heterochromatin is packed so densely that free molecules of GFP do not penetrate into these nuclear regions.
source: In inverted rod nuclei, the chromatin of the central chromocenter (arrows) and the surrounding shell of LINE-rich heterochromatin (arrowheads) is packed so densely that free molecules of GFP do not penetrate into these nuclear regions.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In conventional nuclei, the entire nucleoplasm, regardless to chromatin nature, is penetrable for GFP with chromocenters showing slightly less permeability.
source: In conventional nuclei, exemplified by ganglion and bipolar cells, the entire nucleoplasm, regardless to chromatin nature, is penetrable for GFP with chromocenters showing slightly less permeability (arrows).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: During first 4–6 weeks of postnatal development, conventional nuclear architecture of rod progenitors is gradually rearranged into inverted one of fully mature rods.
source: During first 4–6 weeks of postnatal development, conventional nuclear architecture of rod progenitors (arrow), characterized by multiple chromocenters adjacent to the nuclear periphery, is gradually rearranged into inverted one of fully mature rods (arrow) with a single central chromocenter surrounded by LINE-rich heterochromatin.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rod nuclei ectopically expressing LBR in adult TG-LBR retina have conventional nuclear organization with chromocenters adjacent to the nuclear lamina.
source: Rod nuclei ectopically expressing LBR (green) in adult TG-LBR retina have conventional nuclear organization with chromocenters adjacent to the nuclear lamina (B) and euchromatin occupying the nuclear interior (C).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Only proportion of rods in TG-LBR retina express LBR and thus maintain conventional nuclei.
source: Note that only proportion of rods in TG-LBR retina express LBR and thus maintain conventional nuclei (arrows). Nuclei of rods not expressing LBR are lacking peripheral tethers of heterochromatin and ultimately undergo inversion (arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Chromocenter number distribution in LBR overexpressing rod nuclei is drastically different from WT mice, and similar to a developing WT pup (P14).
source: Chromocenter number distribution in LBR overexpressing rod nuclei is drastically different from WT mice, and similar to a developing WT pup (P14).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Side scattering assessed by FACS for TG-LBR retina nuclei is higher than that of WT nuclei and comparable to that of a WT P14 nuclei with similar chromocenter numbers.
source: Side scattering assessed by FACS for TG-LBR retina nuclei is higher than that of WT nuclei and comparable to that of a WT P14 nuclei with similar chromocenter numbers.
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Excess scattering occurs in multi-chromocenter nuclei models.
source: Excess scattering occurring in multi-chromocenter nuclei models.
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The three photoreceptor layers, represented by photoreceptor perikarya (ONL), cytoplasm of inner segments (IS) and dendritic ends of outer segment (OS), are preserved in TG-LBR retina.
source: The three photoreceptor layers, represented by photoreceptor perikarya (ONL), cytoplasm of inner segments (IS) and dendritic ends of outer segment (OS), are preserved in TG-LBR retina.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Retinal contrast transmission at visually relevant spatial frequencies shows on average ~49% and ~37% better contrast transfer by the WT Adult retina in comparison to the WT-P14 pup and TG-LBR Adult respectively.
source: Retinal contrast transmission at visually relevant spatial frequencies showcasing on an average ~49% and~37% better contrast transfer by the WT Adult retina (grey) in comparison to the WT-P14 pup (blue) and TG-LBR Adult (red) respectively.
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The optical quality improvement of the retina (relative Strehl ratios), as caused by nuclear inversion, is two-fold.
source: The optical quality improvement of the retina (relative Strehl ratios), as caused by nuclear inversion, is two-fold (p=1.1880e-08 - WT adult vs WT pup, 3.4055e-08 - WT adult vs TG-LBR adult, 0.4761 - TG-LBR adult vs WT pup).
evidence: This is based on Strehl ratio calculations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Resolution in transmitted images as assessed by the FWHM of the PSF is comparable between WT and TG-LBR retinae.
source: Comparable resolution in transmitted images as assessed by the FWHM of the psf (inset).
evidence: This is based on PSF measurements shown in Figure 3E2 inset.

claim: Near identical diffuse light transmission occurs in both WT and TG-LBR retinae.
source: Near identical diffuse light transmission by both WT and TG-LBR retinae (n = 2 animals each, mean ± s.d.)
evidence: This is based on transmission measurements shown in Figure 3E3.

claim: Consistent intensity differences of two or more color shades indicate significantly better predator detection potential for WT mice.
source: Consistent intensity differences of two or more color shades indicate significantly better predator detection potential for WT mice.
evidence: This is based on micro-projection experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Transgenic and WT animals showed comparable visual sensitivity at photopic light conditions.
source: Transgenic and WT animals showed comparable visual sensitivity, as quantified by the area under the log-contrast sensitivity curve (AULC, Figure 4B, left) (Villegas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4B (left).

claim: Under scotopic conditions (20 and 2 mLux) the overall sensitivity of the WT mice is 22% and 29% higher than TG-LBR mice.
source: Under scotopic conditions (20 and 2 mLux) the overall sensitivity of the WT mice is 22% and 29% higher than TG-LBR mice (area under log contrast sensitivity curve, AULC) mean+/-95% CI, (p=0.00081, 0.0047, two sample t-test).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4C. Note: The text mentions 18% and 27%, while the figure legend states 22% and 29%.

claim: Significant differences in contrast sensitivity appear at angular sizes above 0.15 cycles/deg.
source: Significant differences appear at angular sizes above 0.15 cycles/deg (p=0.038, two sample t-test).
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mice in possession of the inverted rod nuclei (WT) possess an up to 10 times higher sensitivity at intermediate contrasts (29% vs 3% correct response in 45–75% contrast range).
source: Here the mice in possession of the inverted rod nuclei (WT) possess an up to 10 times higher sensitivity at intermediate contrasts (29% vs 3% correct response in 45–75% contrast range), and a six times reduced risk to miss a motion stimulus at high contrasts (10 vs 59% failure in detection, 0.26–0.3 cycles/deg), (p<0.0001, Chi-square test) mean ± s.d.
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: WT mice have a six times reduced risk to miss a motion stimulus at high contrasts (10 vs 59% failure in detection, 0.26–0.3 cycles/deg).
source: Here the mice in possession of the inverted rod nuclei (WT) possess an up to 10 times higher sensitivity at intermediate contrasts (29% vs 3% correct response in 45–75% contrast range), and a six times reduced risk to miss a motion stimulus at high contrasts (10 vs 59% failure in detection, 0.26–0.3 cycles/deg), (p<0.0001, Chi-square test) mean ± s.d.
evidence: This is based on optomotor response measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Adjusting the level of contrast at the photoreceptor level (by pre-compensation of differential contrast loss) restores sensitivity of TG-LBR mice.
source: Rescue experiment demonstrating sufficiency of improved retinal contrast transmission to explain improved sensitivity. Adjusting the level of contrast at the photoreceptor level (by pre-compensation of differential contrast loss) restores sensitivity of TG-LBR mice.
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The visual response of the TG-LBR mouse is recovered to the level of WT mouse by a stimulus with higher input image contrast compensating for the greater loss due to its ONL with highly scattering non-inverted nuclei.
source: The visual response of the TG-LBR mouse is recovered to the level of WT mouse by a stimulus with higher input image contrast compensating for the greater loss due to its ONL with highly scattering non-inverted nuclei.
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The overall size of the eye as measured by length of the eye along the anterior-posterior (A–P) axis and the naso-temporal (N–T) or superior-inferior (S–I) axes are comparable for WT and TG-LBR adult mice.
source: The overall size of the eye as measured by length of the eye along the anterior - posterior (A–P) axis and the naso-temporal (N–T) or superior-inferior (S–I) axes (N = 9 eyes each) and (B) the measured diameter of the lens (N = 19 lens each) are comparable for WT and TG-LBR adult mice.
evidence: This is based on anatomical measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The measured diameter of the lens is comparable for WT and TG-LBR adult mice.
source: The overall size of the eye as measured by length of the eye along the anterior - posterior (A–P) axis and the naso-temporal (N–T) or superior-inferior (S–I) axes (N = 9 eyes each) and (B) the measured diameter of the lens (N = 19 lens each) are comparable for WT and TG-LBR adult mice.
evidence: This is based on anatomical measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The fusion of heterochromatic chromocenters reduces the volume-specific scattering mainly at large angles.
source: The fusion of heterochromatic chromocenters reduces the volume-specific scattering mainly at large angles.
evidence: This is based on FACS measurements, simulations, and theoretical calculations shown throughout the manuscript, summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reduction in light scattering leads to a near two-fold improvement in the contrast transmission by the retina.
source: Reduction in light scattering leads to a near two-fold improvement in the contrast transmission by the retina.
evidence: This is based on MTF measurements and Strehl ratio calculations shown in Figure 3D, summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Improved image quality transmitted by the retina enables greater contrast sensitivity exclusively at nocturnal conditions.
source: Improved image quality transmitted by the retina finally enables greater contrast sensitivity exclusively at nocturnal conditions.
evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments showing differences only at scotopic light levels (Figure 4C, D, E), summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.
